intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can say what OpenID Connect adds to OAuth, tell an ID token from an access token and say who may accept each, validate an ID token the way the specification lists it, explain what nonce, at_hash and the UserInfo sub comparison each bind, and state what a valid ID token does not prove.

Before you start. You should have read module 4, OAuth basics, for the authorization code flow and PKCE, and module 5, JWT validation, for signatures, algorithms and the idea of a token profile. This module builds on both and repeats neither. SAML is another federation protocol. Module 37 covers it.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleAir's customers sign in to its web app through ExampleAir's own login service. Company names are fictional.

The login service is an OpenID provider (OP): an authorization server that also implements OpenID Connect. The web app is a relying party (RP): an OAuth client that asks the provider to authenticate the user for it. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 calls the protocol "a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol". A client turns an OAuth request into an OpenID Connect request by adding the scope value openid. In return it gets a second token next to the access token: the ID token, a JWT.

The two tokens answer different questions, for different readers:

QuestionAccess tokenID token
What it saysWhat this client may do at an APIThat a user authenticated, when, and how
Who reads and validates itThe API. RFC 9068 section 6: "The client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token"The client. Core section 2 says of its aud: "It MUST contain the OAuth 2.0 client_id of the Relying Party as an audience value."
Where it is sentTo the API and to the provider's UserInfo endpoint, as a bearer credentialNowhere. It stops at the client. The one exception is back to the provider that issued it, as an id_token_hint.
What marks it, when it is a JWTUnder the RFC 9068 profile, header typ of at+jwt, aud naming the API, a scopeaud naming the client, nonce, auth_time

Mixing the two up, or accepting either one from the wrong place, is the attack. A worked example. Alice once signed in to ExampleAir's offers site, a second and less important client of the same provider. That login produced an ID token: issued by ExampleAir's provider, about Alice, for the client exampleair-offers. The token leaked. Mallory sends it to the web app's login callback. The web app checks the signature. It is valid, because the provider really did sign that token. The web app reads the user from it, finds Alice's account and starts a session. Mallory is now Alice in the web app. Nothing was forged and no password was guessed.

Each row below is the same idea with a different token or a different missing check. The first and last columns are results from the lab in section 7. So is the middle column, for the ten rows the lab counts as attacks in its Part J. The second row is not one of those ten: its middle cell is the measured result of exercise 4 in section 8.

Mallory tries toNaive: any token one of the platform's keys verifiesSignature only, each verifier holding one keyFull validation (section 3)
Send Alice's ID token to the bookings API as a bearer tokenWorksBlockedBlocked
Log in to the web app with an access token issued to another clientWorksBlockedBlocked
Replay an ID token issued for another clientWorksBlockedBlocked
Present an ID token from another issuer that reuses Alice's subWorksBlockedBlocked
Put Alice's stolen authorization code into a login in Mallory's own browserWorksWorksBlocked
Use an ID token two hours after it was issuedWorksWorksBlocked
Delete max_age from a request that asks for a recent login, so a stale session passesWorksWorksBlocked
Present a token whose aud lists two clients and whose azp is the other oneWorksBlockedBlocked
Swap the access token in a hybrid-flow redirect for Alice'sWorksWorksBlocked
Call UserInfo with Alice's access token from inside Mallory's own loginWorksWorksBlocked
Write an unsigned token with alg set to noneWorksBlockedBlocked

Read the middle column with care. It is the lab's model, in which every verifier holds a different key (section 3 says why). There, a signature check alone stops six rows, as a side effect of who holds which key. The five rows it leaves open are about time, about the browser session, and about which other token came along. No key can answer those.

In the usual deployment the provider signs with one private key, and every client and every API verifies with the same public key. This project's reasoning, which the lab cannot measure because it has no asymmetric keys: there a signature can verify at every party, so the first three rows and the azp row can behave like the first column, and only the claims separate one client from another and a client from an API. RFC 9068 section 5 says as much for an API: resource servers "have to accept signatures performed with any of the keys published in AS metadata or OpenID Connect discovery". Module 5's lab has the first row with real RSA keys, where one key signs the ID token and the access tokens: its check 12 refuses the ID token for its type.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
OAuth was not built to tell a client who the user is. RFC 6749 section 10.16 says: "Authenticating resource owners to clients is out of scope for this specification." OpenID Connect adds that. What it adds is one more signed token, with rules of its own. Six broken assumptions:

  • "Our provider signed it, so it is a login." A signature says the provider issued the token and nobody changed it. It does not say for whom the token was issued, for which login, or when. Those are claims inside the token: aud, nonce, exp and auth_time. A verifier that stops at the signature accepts every token the provider has ever signed for anyone.
  • "A JWT from our provider is a JWT from our provider." The provider issues at least two kinds. RFC 9068, the profile for JWT access tokens, says its layout "is very similar to that of the id_token", and that its explicit type "helps the resource server to distinguish between JWT access tokens and OpenID Connect ID Tokens". RFC 8725 section 2.8 names the general problem cross-JWT confusion: tokens "issued for one purpose being subverted and used for another". An ID token sent to an API is one direction. The other direction is a client that signs a user in on the strength of an access token. Module 4 names that problem in its section 5 and this module does not repeat it. The Internet-Draft of OAuth 2.1 (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16, a draft and not a standard) puts the reason in one line: "OAuth is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol".
  • "The response came back to the browser that started the login, so it belongs to that login." The state value proves that the redirect returned to the browser session that sent the request. It is a value the browser carries. It says nothing about the authorization code next to it. Mallory, in her own browser, has her own valid state and can change everything else in her own redirect.
  • "The token has not expired, so the user is here." exp is about the token. Core section 2 adds a note, quoted here as written: "The ID Token expiration time is unrelated the lifetime of the authenticated session between the RP and the OP." When the user last proved who they are is a different claim, auth_time, and it can be hours older than the token.
  • "What arrives next to the ID token is about the same user." An access token or a code that travels through the browser can be swapped. Core section 16.11 calls this token substitution: "a class of attacks in which a malicious user swaps various tokens". The ID token is signed. The values beside it are not.
  • "The email address tells us who it is." Core section 5.7: "the only guaranteed unique identifier for a given End-User is the combination of the iss Claim and the sub Claim". It says other claims such as email "MUST NOT be used as unique identifiers for the End-User". A sub is the provider's subject identifier for a user, and it means something only together with the issuer that assigned it.

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
The login, from request to session

OpenID Connect Core calls the request an Authentication Request: "an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request that requests that the End-User be authenticated by the Authorization Server" (section 3.1.2.1). In the authorization code flow it is module 4's request with three additions:

GET /authorize
  ?response_type=code            the authorization code flow
  &scope=openid bookings:read    openid makes this an OpenID Connect request
  &client_id=exampleair-web
  &redirect_uri=https://www.exampleair.example/callback
  &state=<random>                ties the redirect to this browser session
  &nonce=<random>                comes back inside the ID token
  &max_age=300                   optional: how old the user's login may be

Line breaks and notes are for this page only. A real request is URL encoded, and carries module 4's PKCE code_challenge as well.

  1. The client stores state and a secret for the nonce in the browser session and sends the browser to the provider. Section 3.1.2.1 requires the scope: "OpenID Connect requests MUST contain the openid scope value." It lists nonce as optional in this flow. Send it anyway (see below).
  2. The provider authenticates the user and obtains consent. How it does that is outside the specification. Module 27, Attacks on authentication endpoints, is about that step.
  3. The provider redirects the browser to the client's redirect URI with a code and the state.
  4. The client's server checks state, then sends the code to the token endpoint over the back channel, authenticating itself. The response holds an access token and, because the scope included openid, an ID token.
  5. The client validates the ID token (next subsection). Until every check has passed it uses neither token.
  6. If it needs more about the user, it calls the UserInfo endpoint with the access token and compares the sub it gets back.
  7. The client creates its own session, for the account that iss and sub together select. From here on the session is the client's, and module 28, Browser sessions, cookies and CSRF, applies.

What the ID token says:

iss        https://login.exampleair.example   who issued it
sub        u-alice                            the user, unique within this issuer only
aud        exampleair-web                     the client it is for
exp        1790000300                         when the client must stop accepting it
iat        1790000000                         when it was issued
auth_time  1790000000                         when the user last authenticated
nonce      <the value from the request>       which browser session asked
acr        https://login.exampleair.example/acr/password   how the user authenticated
at_hash    <half a hash of the access token>  which access token came with it

Core section 2 requires iss, sub, aud, exp and iat in every ID token. The others appear when they were asked for or when the flow needs them. The acr value is made up for the lab.

Validate the ID token

Section 3.1.3.7 of OpenID Connect Core lists the checks for the code flow. It opens: "Clients MUST validate the ID Token in the Token Response in the following manner". Sections 3.2.2.11 and 3.3.2.12 apply the same list, with two changes noted below, to an ID token that arrived in a redirect. The specification states each item at its own strength, and this list keeps them. Where this course asks for more than the specification does, the item says Baseline. The specification's list begins with decrypting an encrypted ID token. This module and its lab leave encryption out.

  1. Algorithm. Compare the header's alg with the one registered for this client. Core: "The alg value SHOULD be the default of RS256 or the algorithm sent by the Client in the id_token_signed_response_alg parameter during Registration." Baseline: any other value is a rejection, and the header never selects the operation. That is module 5's rule.
  2. Issuer. "The Issuer Identifier for the OpenID Provider (which is typically obtained during Discovery) MUST exactly match the value of the iss (issuer) Claim." Compare it with the issuer this login was started at, as an exact string.
  3. Audience. The client must validate that aud contains its own client_id. aud may be an array. "The ID Token MUST be rejected if the ID Token does not list the Client as a valid audience, or if it contains additional audiences not trusted by the Client."
  4. azp, the authorized party. The specification does not require a check here. It says a client using an extension that produces azp should validate it as that extension says, and: "This validation MAY include that when an azp (authorized party) Claim is present, the Client SHOULD verify that its client_id is the Claim Value." Section 2 adds that "implementations not using such extensions are encouraged to not use azp and to ignore it when it does occur". Baseline: if azp is present and is not your client_id, reject. A token issued to another party is not a login at yours.
  5. Signature. In the code flow the ID token comes straight from the token endpoint, and for that case "the TLS server validation MAY be used to validate the issuer in place of checking the token signature". For every other case: "The Client MUST validate the signature of all other ID Tokens", and "The Client MUST use the keys provided by the Issuer." Baseline: validate the signature every time.
  6. Expiry. "The current time MUST be before the time represented by the exp Claim." Section 2 allows a margin for clock skew: "Implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes". Baseline: 60 seconds. The leeway is time in which an expired token still works, so it should be no larger than the clock error it covers.
  7. Issue time. The specification sets no requirement. It says: "The iat Claim can be used to reject tokens that were issued too far away from the current time, limiting the amount of time that nonces need to be stored to prevent attacks." Baseline: refuse an ID token issued more than 10 minutes ago. The client validates an ID token once, moments after the provider issues it, so an older one is not the answer to a login in progress. exp alone is whatever lifetime the provider chose.
  8. nonce. If the request sent one, "a nonce Claim MUST be present and its value checked to verify that it is the same value as the one that was sent in the Authentication Request". Then, at lower strength: "The Client SHOULD check the nonce value for replay attacks."
  9. acr. "If the acr Claim was requested, the Client SHOULD check that the asserted Claim Value is appropriate." What a value means is for the client and the provider to agree. The specification leaves it out of scope.
  10. auth_time. If it was requested, directly or with max_age, "the Client SHOULD check the auth_time Claim value and request re-authentication if it determines too much time has elapsed since the last End-User authentication". The provider's side is a requirement: when the elapsed time exceeds max_age, "the OP MUST attempt to actively re-authenticate the End-User", and "When max_age is used, the ID Token returned MUST include an auth_time Claim Value."

The lab's validate_id_token runs these ten steps in this order, then the two hash checks described further down, and each returns its own reason. Two notes on the order. Core lists the issuer and the audience before the signature. They decide which key verifies it. The lab puts the algorithm in front of everything, so that nothing in the token chooses how the token is checked. RFC 7519 section 7.2 says of JWT validation in general: "The order of the steps is not significant in cases where there are no dependencies between the inputs and outputs of the steps."

A client sends max_age or acr_values to ask for a recent or a stronger login before a sensitive action. This module calls that a step-up request. Steps 9 and 10 exist because the request travels through the browser. A person at an unlocked computer can delete max_age or acr_values from the address bar, and the provider then has nothing to enforce. Core section 16.20 notes that those two parameters give more assurance when they are sent in a signed request. The check in the ID token is what the client can always do: the lab's checks 33 and 34.

nonce, state and PKCE

Three random values travel with one login. They are easy to confuse and they are not interchangeable.

QuestionstatePKCEnonce
Who makes itThe clientThe clientThe client
How it comes backIn the redirect, as a plain parameterIt does not. The client sends the verifier with the code.Inside the signed ID token
Who checks itThe client, at the callbackThe provider, at the token endpointThe client, when it validates the ID token
What it bindsThe redirect to the browser sessionThe code to the client instance that asked for itThe ID token to the browser session
What it does not doSay anything about the code or the tokensCover tokens that arrive in the redirect. It guards the code exchange only.Stop the provider issuing tokens for a stolen code. The client finds out afterwards.

The replay that nonce stops. Alice's redirect, with her code, leaks before her client redeems it. Mallory starts a login of her own in her own browser, and replaces the code in her redirect with Alice's. Her state is her own and passes. The client redeems Alice's code, with its own valid client authentication, and the provider returns Alice's ID token. A client that does not check nonce signs Mallory in as Alice. A client that does finds Alice's nonce in the token and Mallory's in the session. RFC 9700 section 4.5.3.2 describes this defence against authorization code injection, and sets two conditions for a client that relies on it. It must validate the nonce in the ID token from the token endpoint even when the redirect carried another ID token, and it "MUST ensure that, unless and until that check succeeds, all tokens (ID Tokens and the access token) are disregarded and not used for any other purpose."

How to bind it. Core section 15.5.2 gives one method for a web server client: "store a cryptographically random value as an HttpOnly session cookie and use a cryptographic hash of the value as the nonce parameter". The lab does that. Section 3.1.2.1 requires that the value cannot be guessed: "Sufficient entropy MUST be present in the nonce values used to prevent attackers from guessing values." Use each nonce for one login. The lab's client forgets the pending login as soon as a response for it arrives (check 26).

Which to use. RFC 9700 section 2.1.1 requires public clients to use PKCE, recommends PKCE for confidential clients, and allows a confidential OpenID Connect client to use nonce in its place. Either value "MUST be transaction-specific and securely bound to the client and the user agent in which the transaction was started". Section 4.5.3.2 adds that "nonce does not protect authorization codes of public clients", because a thief can take a public client's code straight to the token endpoint. The OAuth 2.1 draft explains the difference in outcome: a provider that enforces PKCE "is able to recognize the authorization code injection attack pre-emptively and avoid issuing any tokens in the first place" (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16, section 7.5.1.1). Baseline for this course: PKCE and nonce on every login, and state as well. They fail at different places, and module 4 teaches the first. For CSRF in general, see module 28.

Tokens that arrive beside the ID token

An ID token can carry two small hashes that tie it to the values delivered with it. at_hash, the access token hash, is "the base64url encoding of the left-most half of the hash of the octets of the ASCII representation of the access_token value" (section 3.1.3.6). c_hash is the same computation over the authorization code. The hash function follows the ID token's alg: SHA-256 for RS256 and for HS256, so 16 octets are kept.

Whether the provider must include them depends on where the ID token is delivered:

response_typeID token delivered byat_hashc_hash
codeThe token endpointOptional (section 3.1.3.6)Not defined for this flow
id_token tokenThe redirectRequired (section 3.2.2.10)No code is issued
code id_tokenThe redirect, then the token endpointOptionalRequired in the one from the redirect (section 3.3.2.11)
code id_token tokenThe redirect, then the token endpointRequired in the one from the redirectRequired in the one from the redirect

On the client's side the strength is lower. For an access token that came in a redirect, section 3.2.2.9 says the client "SHOULD" recompute the hash, and then "The value of at_hash in the ID Token MUST match the value produced in the previous step." Section 3.3.2.10 says the same for c_hash, when it is present. In the code flow, section 3.1.3.8 says only that the client "MAY use it to validate the Access Token". Section 3.3.3.6 gives the reason, where it lets the hybrid flow's second ID token leave the hashes out: tokens from the token endpoint "are already cryptographically bound together by the TLS encryption performed by the Token Endpoint". Baseline: beside a token or code from a redirect, a missing hash is a rejection, because the provider was required to send it.

What the hashes bind. This access token, or this code, was issued together with this ID token. Without them, RFC 9700 section 4.6.1 says of access token injection that "There is no way to detect such an injection attack in pure-OAuth flows since the token is issued without any binding to the transaction or the particular user agent." With at_hash, it continues, "The attacker therefore needs to replace both the access token as well as the ID Token in the response."

What they do not prove. That the access token is still valid, what it allows, or which API it is for. The lab's check 51 shows an at_hash that still matches an access token the API has stopped accepting. They also say nothing about the browser session. That is the job of nonce. And in the code flow, where they are optional, their absence means nothing.

UserInfo. Core section 5.3 defines the UserInfo endpoint: it "is an OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource that returns Claims about the authenticated End-User". The client sends the access token and gets back a JSON object, which is not signed unless the client registered for a signed response. Section 5.3.2 warns that "the UserInfo Response is not guaranteed to be about the End-User identified by the sub (subject) element of the ID Token", and sets the rule: "The sub Claim in the UserInfo Response MUST be verified to exactly match the sub Claim in the ID Token; if they do not match, the UserInfo Response values MUST NOT be used." The reason is the same substitution. The access token decides whose profile comes back, and the access token is the thing that can be swapped. The provider's half of the rule: "The sub (subject) Claim MUST always be returned in the UserInfo Response."

Algorithms and keys

The default is asymmetric. The default alg for an ID token is RS256. Core section 15.1 says "OPs MUST support signing ID Tokens with the RSA SHA-256 algorithm", with one narrow exception for providers that only allow none. The client gets the provider's public keys from its JWKS, which is module 6, JWKS, revocation and introspection. Core section 2 keeps the token from supplying its own key: "ID Tokens SHOULD NOT use the JWS or JWE x5u, x5c, jku, or jwk Header Parameter fields."

A symmetric algorithm is allowed, for some clients. With HS256 the signature is an HMAC, and section 10.1 names the key: "The MAC key used is the octets of the UTF-8 representation of the client_secret value." The key is a shared secret, so two rules follow. "Symmetric signatures MUST NOT be used by public (non-confidential) Clients because of their inability to keep secrets." And the secret must be long enough: section 16.19 says "for HS256, the client_secret value MUST contain at least 32 octets". Two more consequences are this project's reasoning. The client holds the signing key, so an HS256 ID token cannot show anyone else that the provider issued it. And the provider must be able to read every client secret, where an asymmetric design stores only public keys. Section 3.1.3.7 adds a gap: "For MAC based algorithms, the behavior is unspecified if the aud is multi-valued."

The lab uses HS256 so that it needs nothing beyond the standard library. It follows section 10.1: each client's ID tokens are signed with that client's secret. Real deployments usually use an asymmetric algorithm, as module 5 teaches. The paragraphs under the second table in section 1 say what that difference changes.

none. Core section 2 permits an unsigned ID token in exactly one situation: "ID Tokens MUST NOT use none as the alg value unless the Response Type used returns no ID Token from the Authorization Endpoint (such as when using the Authorization Code Flow) and the Client explicitly requested the use of none at Registration time." This project reads it as resting on the same reasoning as step 5: a token read from the client's own TLS connection to the token endpoint did not pass through anyone else. A client should still refuse none. The exception covers one path, and a validator is rarely called from only one path. The same function ends up checking a token from a redirect, or one posted by the app's own front end, and section 3.1.3.7 requires a signature check for every ID token that did not come directly from the token endpoint. RFC 8725 section 3.2 says the algorithm "should only be used when the JWT is cryptographically protected by other means", and RFC 7518 section 3.6: "Implementations MUST NOT accept Unsecured JWSs by default." Module 5 has the attack. The lab's checks 60 and 61 show the one permitted path and the path next to it.

Discovery and the issuer

A client learns a provider's endpoints from its discovery document. OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 section 4: "OpenID Providers supporting Discovery MUST make a JSON document available at the path formed by concatenating the string /.well-known/openid-configuration to the Issuer." The document is fetched over TLS with the certificate checked, and it names the authorization, token and UserInfo endpoints and the jwks_uri.

The issuer match rule has three parts that must be the same string. Section 4.3: "The issuer value returned MUST be identical to the Issuer URL that was used as the prefix to /.well-known/openid-configuration to retrieve the configuration information. This MUST also be identical to the iss Claim value in ID Tokens issued from this Issuer." Section 7.2 gives the attack the rule stops: someone publishes a document that names the real provider as issuer and lists their own endpoints and keys, which "would enable it to issue ID Tokens as that OP, if accepted by the RP". The lab's check 2 is a look-alike host doing that.

The match is exact, and the path counts. Core section 16.15 says the path component is part of the issuer identifier, so the same subject under an issuer URL with a different path is a different user.

More than one provider. A client that accepts logins from several issuers must remember which one each login was started at. RFC 9700 section 4.4.2: "clients MUST store, for each authorization request, the issuer they sent the authorization request to and bind this information to the user agent". The lab's checks 18 to 21 show why. A second provider can put any sub it likes in its own tokens, including one that belongs to somebody else at the first provider. The token is valid. It is refused in a login that began at the first provider, and in a login that began at the second it selects a different account, because the account key is the pair.

Baseline: write the issuer URL into the client's configuration. If a user can type an identifier that decides where the client fetches a document from, that fetch is a request to an address an outsider chose, which is the subject of module 14, SSRF and unsafe consumption of APIs.

Tokens in the redirect: the implicit and hybrid flows

OpenID Connect Core defines two other ways to deliver tokens. In the implicit flow, "all tokens are returned from the Authorization Endpoint; the Token Endpoint is not used" (section 3.2). In the hybrid flow a code and some tokens come back from the authorization endpoint, and the rest from the token endpoint. In both, the tokens travel in the redirect, through the front channel: section 3.2.2.5 says "all response parameters are added to the fragment component of the Redirection URI", unless the request specified a different response mode, which this module does not cover. The lab prints what the browser can see for each response type:

response_typeFlowIn the redirect, visible to the browser
codeAuthorization codecode, state
code id_tokenHybridcode, ID token, state
code id_token tokenHybridaccess token, code, ID token, state
id_token tokenImplicitaccess token, ID token, state

Core says of the implicit flow that the tokens "are returned directly to the Client, which may expose them to the End-User and applications that have access to the End-User's User Agent". Because nothing in such a redirect can be trusted on arrival, the two changes for an ID token from a redirect are both stricter: its signature must be validated, with no TLS alternative, and the nonce is required, not optional (sections 3.2.2.1, 3.2.2.11 and 3.3.2.1).

What RFC 9700 says. Section 2.1.2 is about access tokens in the redirect: "clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type token) or other response types issuing access tokens in the authorization response", unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage it lists is mitigated. It then says clients should use the response type code, "or any other response type that causes the authorization server to issue access tokens in the token response, such as the code id_token response type". So RFC 9700 recommends against id_token token and code id_token token, and leaves code id_token open. For apps that run in the browser, RFC 10017 section 7.2 is stricter: "the authorization server MUST NOT issue access tokens in the authorization response and MUST issue access tokens only from the token endpoint", and "Browser-based clients MUST use the Authorization Code grant type and MUST NOT use the Implicit grant type to obtain access tokens." The OAuth 2.1 draft omits the implicit grant, and notes that this "does not have an effect on other extension response types returning other artifacts from the authorization endpoint", with response_type=id_token as its example (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16, section 10.1).

An ID token in a URL is still exposed. None of those texts forbids an ID token in the redirect. This project's reasoning for avoiding it anyway: the token holds the user's identifier and often personal data, it sits in the fragment where the page's scripts can read it, and it stays valid until exp at any verifier that skips the checks in this section. RFC 10017 section 9.1 gives the matching advice for the provider: "The authorization server SHOULD NOT include any ID Token claims that aren't used by the client." RFC 9700 section 4.7.1 adds a limit on nonce itself: when an ID token is returned in the authorization response, an attacker who can read that response can take the nonce out of it and use it in a new request.

OpenID Connect Core became final in February 2014, the text with errata set 2 is dated December 2023, and it still says in section 15.4 that the implicit flow "may be appropriate" for a public client. RFC 9700 is from January 2025 and says in its introduction that it sets requirements beyond those of OpenID Connect. Where they differ, this course follows the newer one.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that the issuer named in iss asserted, at the time in iat, to the client named in aud, that the user it calls sub authenticated at auth_time in the way acr describes, and, when the nonce matches, that the token answers the login this browser session started.

Doesn't prove any authorization at an API. An ID token has no scope and its audience is the client. An API that accepts one has skipped its own token check. What the client may do at an API is in the access token, and the resource server validates that.

Doesn't prove the user's rights on any object. Knowing that the caller is Alice does not say whether booking bkg-2001 is hers. That is object-level authorization, in module 9, Object-level authorization, and it happens on every request, long after the login.

Doesn't prove anything after it was issued. The token is a statement about one moment. If Alice logs out at the provider a minute later, or her account is disabled, nothing in the token changes and the client's session carries on. The client learns of it only by asking again: a new authentication request, which can use prompt=none to ask without showing a page, or a max_age on a sensitive step. Core section 15.7 lists four optional specifications about sessions and logout. This module did not read them and does not teach them. For access tokens, revocation is in module 6.

Doesn't prove how good the authentication was, unless the client asked for an acr, the provider and the client agreed what the value means, and the client checked it.

An ID token is a receipt for one login. It is not a session and it is not a permission. Validate it once, at the callback, create your own session, and then put it away. Do not forward it to an API, and do not accept one from a caller.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A working client must refuse every one of these at its login callback, and create no session:

  • An ID token whose aud is another client of the same provider.
  • An ID token whose aud lists this client and one it does not trust, and one whose azp is another client.
  • An ID token whose iss differs from the issuer this login was started at, by a different host, a different path or a trailing slash.
  • A valid response delivered to a browser session that started no login, delivered twice, or carrying a code from another session.
  • An ID token with no nonce when the request sent one.
  • An ID token past exp by more than the leeway, and one issued longer ago than the accepted age.
  • After a request with max_age, an ID token with no auth_time or one that is too old. After a request for an acr, a token with a different one.
  • An unsigned token with alg set to none, a token with any alg other than the registered one, and a token signed with a key that is not the provider's.
  • In a hybrid flow, a redirect whose access token or code does not match at_hash or c_hash, and one with the hash missing.
  • An access token offered where an ID token is expected.

The rest of the system has its own list:

  • The client discards a UserInfo response whose sub is not the ID token's sub.
  • The client refuses a discovery document whose issuer is not the URL it was fetched from.
  • Every API refuses an ID token as a bearer token, with its type check and again without it.
  • The provider refuses response_type values that put an access token in the redirect, and refuses to register HS256 for a public client.
  • Two users with the same email at two issuers get two accounts.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/oidc_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3. The provider, two clients, the API and the browser sessions are Python objects. Nothing opens a socket, and the time is a number the lab sets. Client secrets are random on every run and are never printed, and no token value is printed.

The lab writes the JWT encoding, decoding and validation by hand, because the validation is the lesson. It signs with HS256 for the reason given in section 3. The web app exists twice, as one registered client with two builds. The naive build checks state and then accepts any token that one of its keys verifies, or whose header says it needs no signature. Its key ring holds every key ExampleAir's platform has, which stands in for a deployment where one public key verifies everything. The correct build is section 3.

Four more simplifications. The lab has no PKCE, which module 4 teaches: with it, the provider would refuse the stolen code in Part D before the client saw a token. Access tokens are signed HS256 with a key the provider shares with the API, where RFC 9068 section 2.1 recommends asymmetric cryptography. Each access token names two audiences, the API and UserInfo, so that one login has one access token. The discovery document holds four members and leaves out some that Discovery requires, jwks_uri among them, because the lab has no public keys.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Your API receives a JWT signed by your own provider. It has not expired and its sub is a real customer. Why is that not enough to serve the request?

Because the provider signs more than one kind of token. An ID token passes all three of those tests. Its audience is a client, it carries no scope, and it was never meant to leave that client. For JWT access tokens that follow its profile, RFC 9068 section 4 requires a resource server to check that the header typ is at+jwt or application/at+jwt and that aud names the resource server. In the lab the API refuses the ID token at check 11 for its type, and at check 12 for its audience.

A client checks state on every callback. What does nonce add?

state ties the redirect to the browser session. It travels as a plain parameter, and an attacker in their own browser has a valid one of their own. nonce comes back inside the signed ID token, so it ties the token, and therefore the code that produced it, to the session. In the lab, Mallory's callback passes the state check (check 23) and fails the nonce check (check 24).

In the lab, a signature check with one key per verifier stops five of the ten attacks. Would the same be true with RS256?

Not for all five. With per-client MAC keys, a token for another client fails the signature because it was signed with another client's secret. With RS256 the provider signs every token with one private key and every party verifies with the same public key, so that token's signature verifies everywhere and only aud, azp and typ tell the verifier it is in the wrong place. A token from another issuer and an unsigned token would still fail a signature check that uses a fixed algorithm and the expected issuer's keys. This is reasoning from how the keys are held. The lab has no asymmetric keys and does not measure it.

Alice's account is disabled at the provider at 10:00. A client validated her ID token at 09:59, and its exp is 10:04. What does the client know at 10:01?

Nothing new. The ID token described 09:59, and the client's session is its own. The session continues until the client's timeout ends it or the client asks the provider again. If a disabled account must lose access quickly, that has to be designed: a short session, a fresh authentication request before sensitive steps, or a logout notification from the provider, which this module does not teach.

sections.heading_text: The right token at the wrong door
sections.html:
ExampleAir's bookings API receives a bearer token. It is a JWT signed by ExampleAir's OpenID provider, it has not expired, and its sub is a real customer. Its aud is exampleair-web and its header has no at+jwt type. What should the API do?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/oidc_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The lab compares every result with the one it expects, so each of these edits also makes it exit 1 and list what differed. None of them needs a package.

1. The nonce is present but never compared

In validate_id_token, delete the two lines that compare the nonce: if not same(claims["nonce"], nonce): and the return "reject: nonce mismatch", None under it. The line above them, which refuses a token with no nonce at all, stays.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 23 prints passes in the published run and still does. Mallory's callback carries her own state. The value she changed is the code, and state says nothing about the code.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 24 goes from reject: nonce mismatch to accept: the correct client redeems Alice's code inside Mallory's session and signs Mallory in as Alice. Check 65 goes from 10 to 9. Every other check in the validator still runs and none of them can see the problem, because the token is genuine, unexpired and issued for this client. Check oidc-04 in the Reference layer asks for the comparison, not only the presence.
  • The provider does refuse a code the second time. Alice's code had not been used: her redirect leaked before her client redeemed it. Module 4's PKCE is the control that would stop this at the provider.
  • Check 27 still prints reject: nonce missing. That is a different line of the validator, and this edit leaves it in place.

2. The clock leeway is set to two hours

A colleague is tired of clock skew errors. Near the top of the lab, change LEEWAY = 60 to LEEWAY = 7200.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 29 does change, but not to accept. The expiry test now passes, and the next test catches the token.
  • Check 31 does not move. It was never an expiry failure: that token has a 24 hour lifetime and is refused for its iat.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 29 goes from reject: expired to reject: issued too long ago: the iat limit, which the specification does not even require, is now the only thing refusing a token two hours past its exp. Check 51 goes from 401 invalid_token: expired to 200 u-mallory: 1 bookings, because the API's access token check uses the same constant and has no second limit behind it. One number, two verifiers. Check oidc-05 in the Reference layer keeps the leeway small for this reason.
  • The lab adds the leeway to exp before comparing, as Core section 2 allows. With 7200 seconds of it, two hours past exp is inside the margin.

3. The hashes are read but not compared

In validate_id_token, change if not same(claims[name], half_hash(value)): to if False:. The loop still runs for at_hash and c_hash, and still refuses a redirect in which one is missing.

What do checks 47 and 48 print?

Every option, and why
  • The swapped code is still caught, one step later and by a different control.
  • Correct. Exit 1, three failures: checks 47, 48 and 65. With the swapped access token (check 47) the client now accepts the redirect. Nothing else in the login refers to the access token from the redirect, so nothing else can notice, and check 46 shows what that token then returns. With the swapped code (check 48) the client goes on to redeem Alice's code, receives Alice's ID token from the token endpoint and refuses it for its nonce. The code has a second control behind it and the access token does not. Check oidc-08 in the Reference layer is about this.
  • The nonce is inside the ID token. A swapped access token changes no ID token, so the nonce still matches.
  • The hashes are present in both redirects. The edit removes the comparison, not the presence test, and check 50 still prints reject: at_hash missing.

4. The naive build is given only its own key

This edit is to the naive side. In main, replace the two lines that build key_ring with key_ring = [web_key]. The naive web client and the naive API now hold one key, the web client's own secret, and still check nothing but a signature.

Check 64 counts the attacks the naive validators accept. What does it print, and is the ID token at the API (check 10) still accepted?

Every option, and why
  • Five is what check 66 leaves open, and check 66 gives the API a different key from the client. This edit gives both the same one.
  • Six would mean the API now refuses Alice's ID token. It does not. See the correct answer.
  • Correct. Exit 1, five failures: checks 14, 16, 18, 38 and 64. The access token for the offers site, the ID token for the offers site, the other provider's token and the token issued to the offers site are all signed with keys the ring no longer holds, so the naive client now refuses them. Three of those were among the ten, so check 64 falls from 10 to 7. Check 10 still prints 200 u-alice: 2 bookings: Alice's ID token is signed with the web client's secret, and the naive API in this lab runs on a platform that holds it. Separate keys help only where they are really separate, and the unsigned token in check 57 needs no key at all. Check oidc-03 in the Reference layer asks where each key comes from.
  • The ring was the only reason four of the naive acceptances happened. Take the other keys away and those signatures stop verifying.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 requires a client to validate the ID token. The issuer identifier "MUST exactly match the value of the iss (issuer) Claim". The client must validate that aud contains its client_id, and the token "MUST be rejected if the ID Token does not list the Client as a valid audience, or if it contains additional audiences not trusted by the Client". "The current time MUST be before the time represented by the exp Claim." If a nonce was sent, the claim must be present and must be checked to be the same value.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 states these at lower strength. The alg should be RS256 or the algorithm the client registered. The client should check the nonce for replay, should check that a requested acr is appropriate, and should check a requested auth_time. Checking that azp is its own client_id is something the validation may include. iat "can be used" to reject old tokens, with no requirement.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 allows TLS server validation in place of the signature check for an ID token received directly from the token endpoint, and requires the client to validate the signature of all other ID tokens, using keys provided by the issuer. Sections 3.2.2.11 and 3.3.2.12 require the signature check, and section 3.2.2.11 the nonce check, for an ID token from the authorization endpoint.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 2 forbids none as the ID token alg unless the response type returns no ID token from the authorization endpoint and the client explicitly requested none at registration. Section 10.1 says the MAC key is the octets of the UTF-8 representation of the client_secret and that symmetric signatures must not be used by public clients. Section 16.19 requires at least 32 octets of client_secret for HS256. Section 15.1 requires providers to support RS256, with the exception it states.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 sections 3.2.2.10 and 3.3.2.11 require the provider to include at_hash when an ID token is issued from the authorization endpoint with an access token, and c_hash when it is issued there with a code. Sections 3.2.2.9 and 3.3.2.10 say the client should validate them. In the code flow section 3.1.3.6 makes at_hash optional and section 3.1.3.8 says the client may use it.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 5.3.2 requires that the sub in the UserInfo response "MUST be verified to exactly match the sub Claim in the ID Token; if they do not match, the UserInfo Response values MUST NOT be used". Section 5.7 says only iss and sub together identify a user and that claims such as email must not be used as unique identifiers.
  • StandardOpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 section 4.3 requires the issuer in the configuration document to be identical to the issuer URL used to retrieve it, and to the iss of ID tokens from that issuer. Section 7.2 requires the relying party to ensure all three match exactly, and to perform TLS certificate checking on the configuration request.
  • StandardRFC 9068 section 2.1 requires JWT access tokens to carry the application/at+jwt media type in typ, and says the value used should be at+jwt. Section 4 requires the resource server to verify that the header value is at+jwt or application/at+jwt and to "reject tokens carrying any other value", and to reject a token whose aud does not name it. Section 6 says the client must not inspect the access token.
  • StandardRFC 8725 section 2.8 requires mitigations where a JWT "could be confused with other kinds of JWTs". Section 3.12 requires validation rules for different kinds of JWT from one issuer to be mutually exclusive. Section 3.11 recommends explicit typing for new uses of JWTs.
  • StandardRFC 9700 section 2.1.1 requires clients to prevent authorization code injection: public clients must use PKCE, PKCE is recommended for confidential clients, and a confidential OpenID Connect client may use nonce in its place. Either value must be transaction-specific and bound to the client and the user agent. Section 4.5.3.2 sets the two conditions for relying on nonce. Section 4.4.2 requires a client that uses more than one authorization server to store the issuer of each authorization request.
  • StandardRFC 9700 section 2.1.2 says clients should not use the implicit grant or other response types that issue access tokens in the authorization response, unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage it names is mitigated. RFC 10017 section 7.2 requires, for browser-based applications, that the authorization server issue access tokens only from the token endpoint and that clients not use the implicit grant to obtain access tokens.
  • StandardDraft, not a standard: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16 omits the implicit grant, and says in section 10.1 that removing response_type=token does not affect extension response types such as response_type=id_token.
  • BaselineAn API accepts only access tokens issued for it. A client accepts only ID tokens issued for it, validates them once at the callback, and never forwards one.
  • BaselineFix the ID token algorithm at registration and compare the header with it before anything else. Validate the signature of every ID token, including those from the token endpoint. Never register none.
  • BaselineSend a fresh nonce with every authentication request, derived from a random value kept in the browser session, together with PKCE and state. Use no token until the nonce comparison has passed.
  • BaselineTrust no additional audience, and reject an azp that is not this client. Refuse an ID token issued more than 10 minutes ago. Allow 60 seconds of clock leeway.
  • BaselineBeside a token or code from a redirect, treat a missing at_hash or c_hash as a rejection.
  • BaselineKey user accounts on iss and sub. Run the client's own session with its own timeouts, and ask the provider again before a sensitive step.
  • BaselineConfigure the issuer URL. Do not derive it from user input.
  • OptionHS256 ID tokens for a confidential client, where the client holding the signing key is acceptable and the secret is random and at least 32 octets.
  • OptionThe hybrid response type code id_token, where a profile requires an ID token in the authorization response. Validate its signature, nonce and c_hash, and then the ID token from the token endpoint as well.
  • OptionRelying on TLS in place of the signature for an ID token read directly from the token endpoint, which Core allows. Choose it only if no other path can reach the same validator.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • ID tokens and access tokens are never accepted in each other's place Every API refuses an ID token as a bearer token. No client signs a user in from an access token. Clients do not forward ID tokens to APIs.
  • The client validates iss and aud of every ID token against its own configuration The issuer is the one this login started at, compared exactly. The audience contains this client, no untrusted audience is listed, and an azp that names another client is refused.
  • The ID token signature is checked with a fixed algorithm and a key from the configured issuer The algorithm is the registered one and none is refused. The key comes from the issuer's published keys or this client's registration, never from the token and never by trying every key held.
  • Every login sends a fresh nonce bound to the browser session, and the client compares it A missing nonce, a different nonce and a second response for the same login are all refused, and no token is used before the comparison passes.
  • Expiry and issue time are enforced with a small leeway An ID token past exp is refused, and so is one issued longer ago than a stated limit. The leeway is seconds or a few minutes, and is not shared carelessly with other verifiers.
  • Step-up requests are checked in the ID token, not assumed from the request After max_age the client checks auth_time, and after acr_values it checks acr. A request parameter that the browser carries can be removed on the way.
  • UserInfo is used only when its sub equals the ID token's sub, and accounts are keyed on iss and sub A mismatching response is discarded whole. Email, phone number and name never select an account.
  • No token is taken from a redirect without its binding checks The authorization code flow is the default and the implicit flow is disabled at the provider. Where a hybrid response is used, at_hash and c_hash are compared, a missing one is a refusal, and the ID token from the token endpoint is validated too.
  • The discovery document's issuer matches the configured issuer exactly The document is fetched over TLS from the configured URL, and a document that names a different issuer is refused. The issuer is not taken from user input.
  • A valid ID token is treated as a record of one login and nothing more Authorization is decided per request by the API. The client's session has its own timeouts and ends on the server, and the design says how a logout or a disabled account at the provider reaches it.

<desc>Top row, left to right: the browser session holds the state value and the nonce secret; the client starts a login with the openid scope and a nonce; the provider's authorization endpoint authenticates the user; the client's callback checks state and redeems the code; the provider's token endpoint returns an ID token and an access token. details.summary: Your API receives a JWT signed by your own provider. It has not expired and its sub is a real customer. Why is that not enough to serve the request?
details.html:
Your API receives a JWT signed by your own provider. It has not expired and its sub is a real customer. Why is that not enough to serve the request?

Because the provider signs more than one kind of token. An ID token passes all three of those tests. Its audience is a client, it carries no scope, and it was never meant to leave that client. For JWT access tokens that follow its profile, RFC 9068 section 4 requires a resource server to check that the header typ is at+jwt or application/at+jwt and that aud names the resource server. In the lab the API refuses the ID token at check 11 for its type, and at check 12 for its audience.

details.summary: A client checks state on every callback. What does nonce add?
details.html:
A client checks state on every callback. What does nonce add?

state ties the redirect to the browser session. It travels as a plain parameter, and an attacker in their own browser has a valid one of their own. nonce comes back inside the signed ID token, so it ties the token, and therefore the code that produced it, to the session. In the lab, Mallory's callback passes the state check (check 23) and fails the nonce check (check 24).

details.summary: In the lab, a signature check with one key per verifier stops five of the ten attacks. Would the same be true with RS256?
details.html:
In the lab, a signature check with one key per verifier stops five of the ten attacks. Would the same be true with RS256?

Not for all five. With per-client MAC keys, a token for another client fails the signature because it was signed with another client's secret. With RS256 the provider signs every token with one private key and every party verifies with the same public key, so that token's signature verifies everywhere and only aud, azp and typ tell the verifier it is in the wrong place. A token from another issuer and an unsigned token would still fail a signature check that uses a fixed algorithm and the expected issuer's keys. This is reasoning from how the keys are held. The lab has no asymmetric keys and does not measure it.

quiz.summary: Your API receives a JWT signed by your own provider. It has not expired and its sub is a real customer. Why is that not enough to serve the request?
quiz.html:
Your API receives a JWT signed by your own provider. It has not expired and its sub is a real customer. Why is that not enough to serve the request?

Because the provider signs more than one kind of token. An ID token passes all three of those tests. Its audience is a client, it carries no scope, and it was never meant to leave that client. For JWT access tokens that follow its profile, RFC 9068 section 4 requires a resource server to check that the header typ is at+jwt or application/at+jwt and that aud names the resource server. In the lab the API refuses the ID token at check 11 for its type, and at check 12 for its audience.

quiz.summary: A client checks state on every callback. What does nonce add?
quiz.html:
A client checks state on every callback. What does nonce add?

state ties the redirect to the browser session. It travels as a plain parameter, and an attacker in their own browser has a valid one of their own. nonce comes back inside the signed ID token, so it ties the token, and therefore the code that produced it, to the session. In the lab, Mallory's callback passes the state check (check 23) and fails the nonce check (check 24).

quiz.summary: In the lab, a signature check with one key per verifier stops five of the ten attacks. Would the same be true with RS256?
quiz.html:
In the lab, a signature check with one key per verifier stops five of the ten attacks. Would the same be true with RS256?

Not for all five. With per-client MAC keys, a token for another client fails the signature because it was signed with another client's secret. With RS256 the provider signs every token with one private key and every party verifies with the same public key, so that token's signature verifies everywhere and only aud, azp and typ tell the verifier it is in the wrong place. A token from another issuer and an unsigned token would still fail a signature check that uses a fixed algorithm and the expected issuer's keys. This is reasoning from how the keys are held. The lab has no asymmetric keys and does not measure it.
